claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys and their quaternary and ternary subsets are primarily governed by stacking fault energy.
Changes in stacking fault energy alter the balance between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Reducing or removing particular elements can induce measurable changes in stacking fault energy.
Elemental substitutions alter the electronic and atomic structure of the FCC lattice.
Substitution-induced changes in electronic and atomic structure change stacking fault energy.
Lower stacking fault energy promotes deformation twinning.
Deformation twinning can enhance ductility.
Deformation twinning can enhance strain hardening.
Higher stacking fault energy favors dislocation slip.
Higher stacking fault energy typically results in higher yield strength.
Higher stacking fault energy reduces the contribution of deformation twinning.
Reduced Mn content is expected to produce higher stacking fault energy.
Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, higher-SFE alloys will exhibit increased yield strength.
Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, higher-SFE alloys will exhibit less deformation twinning.
Higher-SFE alloys may exhibit reduced strain-hardening rates.
Lower-SFE alloys should exhibit more prevalent deformation twinning.
The relationship between small composition changes, stacking fault energy, and mechanical properties may be nonlinear.
Microstructural factors other than stacking fault energy may affect the mechanical properties.
The proposed scope is limited to single-phase FCC alloys produced with comparable thermomechanical processing.
Identically processed quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys can be compared using SFE, twinning, dislocation-structure, and tensile-property measurements.
